lines.text: A tiny piece of metal opens your door. But a lock has no idea what your key looks like. It only checks one thing. What?
Inside is a cylinder you turn, called the plug. Pairs of tiny pins, pushed down by springs, straddle the gap between the plug and the housing and lock it in place.
Slide in the right key, and each cut lifts its pins to exactly the right height, so every pair meets right at the gap. That line is called the shear line.
Now nothing blocks the plug. It turns, the bolt slides back, and the door opens. A wrong key leaves one pin straddling the gap, and the plug stays stuck.
Quick test. A typical lock has five pins, with six possible heights each. How many different keys exist? A, fifty. B, about eight thousand. Or C, about eight million? Think!
About eight thousand. Six times six times six times six times six. A lock is a deterrent, not a vault.
Two tips. Never oil a lock, it traps dust and gums up. Use dry graphite or Teflon lubricant instead. And cut new keys from the original, because copies of copies slowly drift out of tolerance.
Watch again, and find the shear line.
